name: Goldenrod
lede: Goldenrod is the strong, slightly mustardy yellow of the flower of that name, and today it is best known as one of the 140 named colors of the web.

sections.title: A flower's yellow
sections.body:
Paterson describes goldenrod as a vivid yellow taken from the plant of the same name, a mustardy color, and one of the 140 colors in the X11 set, with the hex code #DAA520 [1]. That is exactly the swatch on this page [1]. St Clair's glossary agrees: a strong yellow, named after the flower [2]. In a footnote on fuchsia she lists goldenrod among the color names taken from flowers [3].

The web gave the name its wide use, but not its first record. Our sources find a goldenrod-like entry in Werner's 1821 nomenclature, where it is no. 76 among the [[orange]] group, and Maerz and Paul date a plate to 1814 [4]. Ridgway's 1912 charts, a German RAL standard of 1927 and the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955, which calls it a strong yellow, 4.6 units away, all carry it [4].

sections.title: Where it sits among the yellows
sections.body: The nearest named color is [[mustard]], only 2.9 units away, which is why Paterson's word for it is mustardy [1][4]. Our library also files Broom Yellow, Aniline Yellow and Turkey Berries as close equals, the last dated 1841 [4]. Set against a pure [[yellow]], goldenrod is deeper and warmer, a yellow with a little brown in it.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Goldenrod is one of the more common named colors in paint: 231 of 23,781 paintings in our archive (0.97 per cent), 247 by the stricter within-painting count, more common than 74 per cent of named colors [5]. It is usually an accent, in 79 per cent of those 247 [5].

It peaks in the 1800s, in 102 of 8,345 paintings, 1.2 times the baseline [5]. The painter most devoted to it is George Dawe, in 9 of his 50 works here, 7.6 times the baseline of the museums those works come from, and by country it is most over-represented in India, 4.4 times, with 54 of 721 paintings [5]. It travels with [[mustard-brown]] more than chance would suggest [5].

The earliest match is a work of 1240, a look-alike hue 581 years before the name's first record in our sources, 1821 [5]. In printed English the adjective peaks in the 1940s and grew fastest in the 1900s [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test. [5]

origin.first_recorded: Werner 1821 in our sources; Maerz & Paul give 1814
